title: Advanced Syllogisms — Three-Statement Deduction
tagline: Year 3 — Three statements and four classes: building chains, Venn diagrams and "definitely follows" tests

introduction.overview: A syllogism asks which conclusions must be true given some statements about classes of things. With three statements and four classes, mental guessing fails, so the method is the Venn-diagram test: draw every diagram that fits the statements, and accept a conclusion only if it holds in all of them. The convention used in this course is that every named class has at least one member.
introduction.placementRelevance: Three-statement syllogisms with two conclusions are a standard logical-reasoning item in company tests.
introduction.realWorldContext: Checking whether a policy follows from several rules, or whether a claim is entailed by a set of facts, uses the same reasoning.

learningObjectives: State the four statement types precisely
Decide "follows" only if true in every diagram

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: "All A are B" puts A inside B. "No A is B" keeps the two circles apart. "Some A are B" means they overlap. "Some A are not B" means part of A is outside B.

coreDefinitions: Follows: true in every possible diagram that fits the statements.
Possible but not forced: true in some diagrams and false in others, so it does not follow.
Contradicts: false in every diagram, so it does not follow and its negation does.
Convention in this course: every class named in a statement has at least one member.
Chain: All A are B and All B are C give All A are C.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: A conclusion follows only if you could not draw a legal diagram that breaks it. Try to break the conclusion; if you succeed, it does not follow.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Draw the statements as circles. Start with the "All" statements (nested circles), add the "No" separation, then the "Some" overlaps. For each conclusion, ask: can I redraw it so the conclusion is false?

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: All chain
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: All A are B, All B are C ⇒ All A are C

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: All + Some
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: All A are B, Some A are C ⇒ Some B are C

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: All + No
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: All A are B, No B is C ⇒ No A is C

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Some + All
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Some A are B, All B are C ⇒ Some A are C

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Some does not chain
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Some A are B, Some B are C ⇏ Some A are C

mainNarrative: Take the statements: All pens are books; All books are tables; Some tables are chairs. The chain gives All pens are tables. The third statement only says that tables and chairs overlap, so nothing definite follows about pens and chairs: "Some pens are chairs" is possible but not forced.

With the statements: Some cats are dogs; All dogs are birds; No birds are fish. Some cats are dogs and all dogs are birds, so Some cats are birds follows. Birds and fish are separate, so dogs and fish are separate: No dogs are fish follows.
A "Some" statement does not pass through another "Some". Some A are B and Some B are C leave A and C free to overlap or not, so "Some A are C" does not follow.

Converses of "All" are traps. From "All doctors are teachers" you cannot conclude "All teachers are doctors". You can conclude "Some teachers are doctors" under the course convention that classes are non-empty.
To test a tempting conclusion, build a diagram that respects all statements but makes it false. If one exists, the conclusion does not follow.

deepDiveAspects.title: Existence convention
deepDiveAspects.content: Under the convention that every class is non-empty, All A are B guarantees Some A are B.

deepDiveAspects.title: Negative statements
deepDiveAspects.content: No A is B is symmetric: No B is A follows. Some A are not B does not give Some B are not A.

solvedExamples.title: Chain
solvedExamples.question: Statements: All pens are books. All books are tables. Does "All pens are tables" follow?

steps.title: Nest again
steps.explanation: Books are inside tables, so pens are inside tables.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Every diagram has pens inside tables.

solvedExamples.title: Two Somes
solvedExamples.question: Statements: Some cats are dogs. Some dogs are birds. Does "Some cats are birds" follow?

steps.title: Break
steps.explanation: Draw the cats–dogs overlap at one part of dogs and the dogs–birds overlap at a different part.

steps.title: Result
steps.explanation: Cats and birds do not overlap in that diagram, so the conclusion can be false.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: It is possible but not forced.

solvedExamples.title: All + No
solvedExamples.question: Statements: All dogs are birds. No birds are fish. Does "No dogs are fish" follow?

steps.title: Separate
steps.explanation: Fish are outside birds, so also outside dogs.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The inner circle cannot touch what the outer one avoids.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Draw the nested and separate circles; for each conclusion try to redraw so it is false. If you can, it does not follow.

commonMistakes.howToAvoid: All A are B does not give All B are A.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Eliminate a conclusion the moment one diagram breaks it.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Draw All statements first, then No, then Some.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Two-conclusion items are quick once you can break conclusions.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I reject a tempting Some?
Can I apply the non-empty convention?
